**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 2 (0760), Paper 2 - Cameroon History Since 1800, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2020. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each of the sections. All the questions carry equal marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Sections: SECTION A (1800 - 1922), questions 1 to 4; SECTION B (1922 - 1961), questions 5 to 8; SECTION C (1961 to present), questions 9 to 12.

Points : chaque question imprime « (25 marks) » et le sujet dit « All the questions carry equal marks » ; `points` vaut donc 25 pour chaque question. Aucun écart constaté entre les points imprimés.

Sujet scanné de deux pages (page de garde, puis les 12 questions) : filigrane et publicités gcerevision.com sans conséquence sur la lisibilité ; aucune question n'est coupée ni illisible. Page de garde vérifiée : « JUNE 2020 », ADVANCED LEVEL, History, Paper 2 - Cameroon History Since 1800, code 0760, trois heures.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées de mémoire historiographique, sans accès à un manuel pendant la rédaction ; aucune statistique ni citation n'est avancée. Les dates et les faits cités sont ceux de l'historiographie courante du Cameroun, mais n'ont pas pu être recoupés avec une source écrite : à relire par un historien avant publication.

Détails de la conférence de Foumban (juillet 1961), de la conférence de Bamenda (juin 1961), répartition des sièges de l'Assemblée fédérale (40 pour l'Est, 10 pour l'Ouest) et procédure de révision constitutionnelle contournée en 1972 cités de mémoire. L'idée que la fédération était, pour Ahidjo, une étape transitoire est présentée comme un débat d'historiens, pas comme un fait.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Why and with what consequences for Southern Cameroons was a federal constitution adopted at Foumban in 1961?

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** In the plebiscite of February 1961, organised by the United Nations, the people of Southern Cameroons voted to achieve independence by joining the Republic of Cameroun (the former French Cameroun), whereas Northern Cameroons voted to join Nigeria. The terms of the union were then negotiated at the **Foumban Constitutional Conference** (in the Bamum capital, July 1961) between the delegation of Southern Cameroons, led by Prime Minister John Ngu Foncha, and the government of President Ahmadou Ahidjo. The conference led to the adoption of a **federal constitution**, which came into force on 1 October 1961, creating the Federal Republic of Cameroon made up of two states, East Cameroon and West Cameroon.

**1. Why a federal constitution was adopted**

- **Southern Cameroons' wish to preserve its identity.** The territory had a British colonial heritage: the English language, the common law, a parliamentary system, its own educational system and administrative traditions, and a House of Chiefs. Its leaders did not wish to be absorbed into a unitary French-style state, and they were afraid of French and Francophone domination, in view of the difference in population (West Cameroon was much smaller than East Cameroon). Federation promised self-government in local matters.
- **Foncha's and the KNDP's policy.** The KNDP had campaigned for reunification on the basis of a federation of two equal states, and in the Bamenda All Party Conference (June 1961) the Southern Cameroons leaders agreed on proposals for a federation. Foncha went to Foumban to obtain a constitution that respected this principle.
- **The attitude of Ahidjo.** Ahidjo was mainly interested in unification itself. He accepted a federal arrangement as a way of winning the Southern Cameroons, of ensuring its integration and of avoiding conflict, and he was willing to give some guarantees to the Anglophones. Many observers think that he regarded federation as a transitional stage, but this view is debated.
- **The practical needs of the two territories.** The differences of administration, law, language and economy between the two territories made a quick merger difficult. Federation was a compromise that allowed time for integration.
- **Time pressure and political circumstances.** The date for reunification (1 October 1961) was close, the conference was short (a few days) and the Southern Cameroons team was not well prepared, so it accepted a compromise that gave the federal government extensive powers. The East Cameroon side had a draft constitution and the majority of the delegates.

**2. Consequences for Southern Cameroons (West Cameroon)**

*Positive consequences*

- **Reunification achieved.** The union ended British rule and separation from Nigeria and fulfilled the wish of the KNDP and many Cameroonians for reunification. West Cameroon became independent as part of a larger state.
- **Self-government and the preservation of institutions.** West Cameroon kept its own Prime Minister and government, House of Assembly, House of Chiefs, judiciary and the common law, and its educational system, and English became an official language together with French (bilingualism).
- **Representation at federal level.** Foncha became Vice-President of the Federal Republic and West Cameroonians had seats in the Federal Assembly and in the federal government.
- **Access to federal resources.** West Cameroon could benefit from federal development funds and from the larger national market, for example for its plantation products, roads and public services.

*Negative consequences*

- **Federal dominance and centralisation.** The federal government controlled defence, foreign affairs, the currency, higher education, and the army and police, and had priority in many fields; the President had large powers, including special powers in an emergency and, later, the appointment of federal inspectors of administration in the states. The autonomy of West Cameroon was progressively reduced, and the East, with its larger population, dominated the Federal Assembly (the East had 40 of the 50 seats).
- **Erosion of the federal system.** The creation of a single party, the Cameroon National Union (1966), the weakening of the regional political parties and Ahidjo's control of appointments reduced the independence of West Cameroon's government. The system was finally abolished in 1972 when a referendum replaced the federation with a unitary state, the United Republic of Cameroon; critics say that this method bypassed the procedure for revising the constitution, which gave a role to the West Cameroon deputies.
- **Loss of Anglophone institutions and marginalisation.** Anglophone Cameroonians later complained of assimilation into the French-speaking system, of the loss of their British-style administration and common law practices, of limited representation in key posts and of economic neglect. These grievances are the roots of the Anglophone problem that has been important in Cameroon politics.
- **Economic dependence.** West Cameroon's financial and economic institutions were gradually integrated into the federal system, and the region became dependent on federal funds and decisions.

**Conclusion.** A federal constitution was adopted at Foumban because West Cameroon's leaders wanted guarantees for their British-inherited institutions and for equality, because Ahidjo wanted unity at any price, and because circumstances left little time for detailed negotiation. For Southern Cameroons it brought reunification, self-government and bilingualism at first, but the strong federal powers and later centralisation undermined its autonomy and prepared the abolition of the federation in 1972, leaving a legacy of Anglophone grievances.
